newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel, Palestinians said close to Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel, Palestinians said close to Hebron deal.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians said they were within hours of a deal on the long-delayed Israeli troop pullback from the West Bank town of Hebron.

"The issues have been resolved," one Palestinian official, who declined to be identified, said as marathon talks went into Friday. "If there are no problems in the drafting, within 24 hours there will be positive results and an agreement."
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross was helping to draft a protocol for implementing the agreement. Palestinians said it could be signed on Friday or Sunday and start coming into force 10 days later.
Israeli and Palestinian negotiators met in Eilat in Israel and Taba in Egypt, neighbouring Red Sea resorts, to hammer out issues and a protocol for implementing the pullback.
"Within hours the matter could be completed," Foreign Minister David Levy told Israel's Channel Two on Thursday.

Israel has held up redeployment in Hebron, citing security concerns for the 400 Jews who live and study in enclaves among 100,000 Arabs. The city is sacred to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
The deployment, due to have taken place in March, was delayed by Islamic suicide bombings in Israel and later put off by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu elected in May.
Palestinians view the Hebron redeployment -- part of a 1995 deal with the previous left-centre Israeli government -- as a litmus test of Netanyahu's commitment to peace.
Late into the night the main talks moved to a hotel in Eilat -- away from the scrutiny of journalists who had assembled in Taba for talks earlier in the day.

The Palestinian official said major stumbling blocks were removed during a meeting on Thursday between Israeli army chief Amnon Shahak, PLO negotiator Abu Mazen, Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbu and Ross.
Palestinian officials said Israel was no longer insisting on establishing a buffer zone or on the right to hot pursuit of wanted Palestinians in areas of Hebron coming under PLO control.
They said it was also agreed that talks on all other outstanding issues in a 1995 interim deal would start immediately after the Hebron agreement was concluded.

These issues would include further redeployments, the release of Palestinian prisoners, safe passage between the West Bank and Gaza Strip, operation of a Gaza airport for Palestinians and allowing more Palestinians to work in Israel.
Also on Thursday, Netanyahu's office declined comment on an Israeli television report that a secret message from Syria could enable their long-stalled peace talks to resume.

A spokeswoman would not comment on the Channel Two report that Netanyahu's political adviser Dore Gold secretly met U.S. diplomat Edward Djerejian who was returning from a meeting with Syrian President Hafez al-Assad in Damascus.
It said they met at the Allenby Bridge connecting the West Bank to Jordan.
Netanyahu insists he is keen to make peace but Arabs are sceptical because he opposes swapping occupied land for peace -- a foundation of their talks launched in Madrid in 1991.
Syria demands the return of all of the Golan Heights captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Netanyahu opposes giving up any of the strategic plateau.

Hawkish Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon told a Tel Aviv University audience the only way to peace was for Palestinian refugees to be resettled in Arab states. Palestinian refugees of wars in 1948 and 1967 demand the right of return.

"The refugees of '48 and also the refugees of '67...are an open wound which, so long as it isn't healed, means there cannot be real peace here. The only way to solve the problem is to resettle them in the Arab states," Sharon said.
